art-synovialis.summary: Freely movable joints with a fluid-filled joint cavity between the bone ends. The articular surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage; a fibrous capsule encloses the joint and a synovial membrane lines it.
facts: Articular cartilage (usually hyaline), joint cavity, joint capsule (fibrous membrane outside, synovial membrane inside), synovial fluid
Ligaments (extracapsular, intracapsular), discs and menisci, labra, fat pads, bursae
A slippery fluid rich in hyaluronic acid produced by the synovial membrane; it nourishes the cartilage and reduces friction
Supplied by arterial networks around the joint; by Hilton's law the nerves supplying the muscles that cross a joint also supply the joint
Articular cartilage has no vessels or nerves; it is nourished by diffusion from the synovial fluid
sections: A bursa is a small sac lined by synovial membrane between structures that rub against each other, such as tendon and bone or skin and bone. Some communicate with the joint cavity (e.g. the suprapatellar bursa). Tendon sheaths (synovial sheaths) wrap long tendons in osteofibrous tunnels; they are prominent around the wrist and ankle.

The stability of a joint depends on three factors: the shape and fit of the articular surfaces (hip), the strength of the ligaments (knee) and the tone of the surrounding muscles (shoulder). Joints with a large range of movement are usually less stable.
clinical: Osteoarthritis involves wear of the articular cartilage; joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis are seen.
Rheumatoid arthritis is chronic inflammation of the synovial membrane; the pannus erodes cartilage and bone.
Bursitis (e.g. prepatellar bursitis – 'housemaid's knee', olecranon bursitis) develops with repeated pressure or friction.
tus: Hilton's law: the nerves supplying the muscles that cross a joint also supply the joint and the skin over it.
Articular cartilage is avascular and has no perichondrium; therefore its damage does not heal.

artt-craniovertebrales.summary: The joints between the skull and the first two cervical vertebrae: the atlanto-occipital joint between the occipital condyles and the atlas, and the atlanto-axial joints between the atlas and the axis. They allow the 'yes' (nodding) and 'no' (turning) movements of the head.
facts: Occipital condyles – superior articular facets of the atlas; ellipsoid synovial joint; flexion-extension of the head ('yes') and slight lateral bending
Median atlanto-axial joint in the middle (dens – anterior arch of atlas and transverse ligament; pivot joint), lateral atlanto-axial joints on each side (plane); rotation of the head ('no')

Cruciform ligament of the atlas (transverse ligament and longitudinal bands), alar ligaments (from the dens to the occipital condyles; limit excessive rotation), apical ligament of the dens, tectorial membrane (continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament), anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membranes
About half of neck rotation takes place at the atlanto-axial joint and a large part of flexion-extension at the atlanto-occipital joint
sections: The most important ligament holding the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas and preventing it from shifting backwards into the spinal cord. If it ruptures, the dens can compress the spinal cord and medulla oblongata.
clinical: In rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome laxity of the transverse ligament can cause atlanto-axial instability and cord compression.
Fractures of the dens (especially type II – base of the dens) are common in falls in the elderly and carry a high risk of non-union.
A burst fracture of the atlas (Jefferson fracture) results from vertical loading on the top of the head.
tus: The atlanto-occipital joint allows the 'yes' movement, the atlanto-axial joint the 'no' movement.
The alar ligaments limit excessive rotation of the head; the tectorial membrane is the continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament up to the skull base.

artt-zygapophysiales.summary: Small synovial joints between the articular processes of adjacent vertebrae (facet joints). The cervical vertebrae also have uncovertebral (Luschka) joints at the lateral margins of the bodies. The orientation of these joints determines the type of movement in each region.
facts: Facet joints: synovial plane joints; uncovertebral joints: cleft-like joints at the lateral margin of the disc

Cervical region near horizontal (inclined front to back) – movement in all directions; thoracic region in the frontal plane – rotation; lumbar region in the sagittal plane – flexion-extension, rotation limited
Medial branches of the posterior rami of the spinal nerves; each facet joint receives fibres from two adjacent levels
Between the uncinate processes on the upper lateral margins of the C3–C7 bodies and the vertebra above
clinical: Facet joint arthrosis is a common cause of back and neck pain; it can be treated by medial branch block or radiofrequency ablation.
Osteophytes of the uncovertebral joints can narrow the intervertebral foramen and cause cervical radiculopathy.
In spondylolysis there is a defect in the pars interarticularis (usually L5); on oblique X-ray it gives the 'collar on the Scottie dog' appearance.
tus: The lumbar facets lie in the sagittal plane, so rotation is limited in the lumbar region; in the thoracic region rotation is free.
The pars interarticularis is the bony bridge between the superior and inferior articular processes; its stress fracture is spondylolysis.

ligg-art-temporomandibularis.tr: Disc and ligaments of the temporomandibular joint
ligg-art-temporomandibularis.summary: The fibrocartilaginous disc inside the temporomandibular joint divides the joint cavity into upper and lower compartments. The joint is supported laterally by the lateral ligament and at a distance by the sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments.
facts: Biconcave fibrocartilage disc; attached in front to the upper head of lateral pterygoid and behind to the bilaminar zone (retrodiscal tissue)
Upper compartment: gliding (translation); lower compartment: hinge (rotation)
From the zygomatic arch to the neck of the mandible; a thickening of the capsule that prevents the condyle from moving backwards
Sphenomandibular ligament (spine of the sphenoid – lingula of the mandible), stylomandibular ligament (styloid process – angle of the mandible), pterygospinous ligament
sections: In the first stage of opening the condyle rotates about its own axis in the lower compartment; on wider opening the condyle and disc glide together forwards in the upper compartment towards the articular tubercle. This forward glide is produced mainly by the lateral pterygoid.
clinical: In temporomandibular disorders the disc may be displaced forwards; there is a click and pain on opening, and in later stages opening locks.
In dislocation of the jaw the condyle slips in front of the articular tubercle and the mouth cannot close; it is reduced by pressing downwards and backwards.
tus: The muscle that pulls the disc forwards is the lateral pterygoid; dislocation of the TMJ is always anterior.
The sphenomandibular ligament is a remnant of the 1st pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage).

artt-costovertebrales.summary: Behind, each rib forms two joints with the vertebrae: the joint of the head of the rib with the vertebral bodies and the costotransverse joint between the tubercle of the rib and the transverse process. These joints allow the ribs to move in breathing.
facts: In typical ribs the head articulates with two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them; reinforced by the radiate ligament and the intra-articular ligament
Tubercle of the rib – transverse process of the vertebra of the same number; reinforced by the costotransverse, superior and lateral costotransverse ligaments (absent in the 11th and 12th ribs)
'Pump-handle' movement in the upper ribs (increases the anteroposterior diameter), 'bucket-handle' movement in the lower ribs (increases the transverse diameter)
clinical: In ankylosing spondylitis involvement of the costovertebral joints reduces chest expansion and lowers respiratory capacity.
tus: The heads of the 1st, 10th, 11th and 12th ribs articulate only with the vertebra of their own number (single facet).
The pump-handle movement increases the anteroposterior diameter of the chest in the upper ribs, the bucket-handle movement the transverse diameter in the lower ribs.

art-sacrococcygea.summary: Small cartilaginous joint between the apex of the sacrum and the base of the coccyx; it is reinforced by a thin disc and ligaments.
facts: Symphysis (secondary cartilaginous joint); may ossify with age
Anterior, superficial and deep posterior and lateral sacrococcygeal ligaments; intercornual ligaments between the sacral and coccygeal cornua
During childbirth the coccyx moves slightly backwards, widening the pelvic outlet
clinical: Coccydynia (tailbone pain) usually develops after a fall in the sitting position or after childbirth, from strain of this joint.
tus: During childbirth the coccyx moves backwards, increasing the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet.

ligg-art-humeri.tr: Ligaments and labrum of the shoulder joint
ligg-art-humeri.summary: The three glenohumeral ligaments on the front of the shoulder capsule, the coracohumeral ligament above and the fibrocartilaginous labrum deepening the rim of the glenoid cavity are the passive stabilisers of the joint.
facts: Fibrocartilaginous ring attached to the rim of the glenoid cavity; deepens the socket by about 50%; the long head of biceps arises from its upper part
Superior, middle and inferior on the front of the capsule; the inferior is the most important and protects against anterior dislocation with the arm in abduction and external rotation
From the coracoid process to the greater and lesser tubercles; reinforces the rotator interval and prevents the arm from slipping downwards
Bridges the intertubercular groove between the greater and lesser tubercles, holding the tendon of the long head of biceps in its groove
The lower part of the capsule (axillary recess) and the rotator interval between subscapularis and supraspinatus
clinical: A Bankart lesion is a tear of the anteroinferior labrum and inferior glenohumeral ligament; it is the main cause of recurrent anterior dislocations.
If the transverse humeral ligament tears, the long head of biceps tendon can slip out of its groove (subluxation) and cause a painful click.
A SLAP lesion is a tear of the superior labrum from front to back; it occurs in throwing sports.
tus: The inferior glenohumeral ligament is the most important static stabiliser against anterior dislocation in abduction and external rotation.
The long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and superior labrum; it runs inside the capsule within a synovial sheath.

ligg-scapulae.tr: Ligaments of the scapula and coraco-acromial arch
ligg-scapulae.summary: Ligaments stretched between parts of the scapula itself. The coraco-acromial ligament forms, with the acromion and coracoid process, a protective arch over the shoulder joint; the transverse scapular ligaments complete the openings through which the suprascapular nerve and vessels pass.
facts: Acromion, coraco-acromial ligament and coracoid process; prevents the humeral head from moving upwards; the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa lie beneath it
Converts the suprascapular notch into a foramen: the suprascapular nerve passes below it, the suprascapular artery and vein above
Between the lateral border of the spine of the scapula and the glenoid cavity; the suprascapular nerve and artery pass beneath it to the infraspinous fossa
Conoid ligament (medial, cone-shaped) and trapezoid ligament (lateral); suspend the clavicle from the scapula and provide vertical stability of the AC joint
clinical: In impingement syndrome the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa are pinched under the coraco-acromial arch as the arm is raised sideways; the painful arc lies between 60 and 120°.
Entrapment of the suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular notch causes wasting of supraspinatus and infraspinatus; at the spinoglenoid notch (inferior ligament) only infraspinatus is affected.
tus: At the suprascapular notch the nerve passes below the ligament and the artery above it ('Army over Navy': artery above, nerve below).
AC dislocations are graded (Rockwood) according to whether the coracoclavicular ligaments are torn.
